etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin rīvālis (literally “person using the same stream as another”), from rīvus (“small stream, brook”).

definitions.definition: A competitor (person, team, company, etc.) with the same goal as another, or striving to attain the same thing. Defeating a rival may be a primary or necessary goal of a competitor.

quote.citation: 1983, “Karma Chameleon”, in Colour by Numbers, performed by Culture Club:
quote.text: Every day is like survival / You're my lover, not my rival

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Oliver Burkeman, “The tao of tech”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 27:
quote.text: The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. Web companies like to boast about […], or offering services that let you […]  "share the things you love with the world" and so on. But the real way to build a successful online business is to be better than your rivals at undermining people's control of their own attention.

definitions.definition: Someone or something with similar claims of quality or distinction as another.
(obsolete) One having a common right or privilege with another; a partner.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus, / The rivals of my watch, bid them make haste.

definitions.definition: Having the same pretensions or claims; standing in competition for superiority.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter I, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: The strenuous conflicts and alternate victories of two rival confederacies of statesmen.

definitions.definition: To be equal to, or match, or to surpass another.

quote.citation: 1941 January, C. Hamilton Ellis, “The Scottish Station”, in Railway Magazine, page 1:
quote.text: But the Waverley is still the best-placed station of any British city, and gives the arriving stranger a first impression rivalled in Europe only by the exclusively watery station approach at Venice.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 1, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: The original family who had begun to build a palace to rival Nonesuch had died out before they had put up little more than the gateway,  […] .

definitions.definition: To strive to equal or excel; to emulate.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: to rival thunder in its rapid course
